summary: Extends the GSS-API for applications that need to protect an individual data unit, such as a file or message, independently of other units and of any live contact with the receiver. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Most security tools protect a conversation. This one protects a single letter or file by itself, so it stays safe even if nobody is on the line.

questions: how can a single message be protected with gss-api
what evidence types does idup support
subtitle: Protecting single messages or files with cryptography independent of any connection.

tldr.problem: The original GSS-API protects data during live connections between peers (like a phone call). Many applications need to protect a single file or message in isolation, to be stored or transmitted at any time without any connection with the recipient.
tldr.mechanism: IDUP-GSS-API extends GSS-API to allow applications to protect Independent Data Units (IDUs) like files or emails with services such as encryption, authentication, and non-repudiation. Protection and unprotection are completely separate operations that need not be coordinated.
tldr.outcome: Applications can implement secure email, document signing, evidence generation, and archival security using a standard API that works with different underlying cryptographic mechanisms.

facts.label: Evidence types supported
facts.value: Proof of origin, creation, sender, delivery, receipt, approval

today: RFC 2479 is Informational and describes an extension to GSS-API for independent data unit protection. While the specification is technically sound, it has not been widely adopted as a standard. Today's secure email and document protection systems typically use their own APIs or simpler cryptographic standards rather than the full IDUP-GSS-API specification. However, the concepts and design patterns remain relevant for applications needing independent protection of multiple data units.

sections.title: Independent Data Unit Protection
sections.content:
The IDUP-GSS-API extends the GSS-API for applications requiring protection of generic data units (such as a file or message) in a way that is completely independent of the protection of any other data unit and independent of any live contact with intended receivers. An Independent Data Unit (IDU) is a stand-alone unit of data whose protection is entirely independent of any other unit. Multiple IDUs sent to a single receiver can be unprotected in any order, at any time, with no logical connection implied by the protection process.

The protection offered by IDUP includes data origin authentication with integrity, confidentiality with integrity, and support for non-repudiation services such as proof of origin and proof of delivery. After protection, the data can be transferred to recipients or to an archive, and processed only days or years later. This makes IDUP suitable for secure email, document archival, and any application where data must be protected without real-time communication with recipients.
sections.eli5: You write a letter, sign and seal it, and put it in the mailbox. The mailman doesn't need to talk to you. Your friend gets it whenever and reads it whenever. That's IDUP in a nutshell.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
IDUP introduces the concept of a Security Environment, which is different from a GSS-API security context. An environment is purely local to the calling application and exists for the purpose of protecting or unprotecting one or more IDUs using a particular credential. Unlike GSS-API contexts which exist between peers, IDUP environments are not shared. An application establishes an environment by calling IDUP_Establish_Env(), performs protection or unprotection operations on IDUs, then calls IDUP_Abolish_Env() to clean up.

During protection, the input IDU buffers may be modified (for example, encrypted or encoded) or may remain unchanged, resulting in a Modified IDU (M-IDU). The protection output, called a Protected IDU (P-IDU), may either encapsulate the M-IDU in a single token or be the logical concatenation of a token and the M-IDU. The RFC specifies that protection operations support both single-buffer (whole IDU in memory) and multi-buffer (streaming) processing for flexibility.
sections.eli5: You set up your workspace with your credentials (IDUP_Establish_Env). You protect things in it. When you're done, you clean up (IDUP_Abolish_Env). Your protected message is ready to send whenever you want.

sections.title: Security Services and Operations
sections.content:
IDUP provides three main groups of per-IDU operations: SE (Sign/Encrypt) calls for simple signing and encryption, EV (Evidence) calls for non-repudiation evidence generation and verification, and GP (General Protection) calls for complex combinations of services. The SE calls provide the simplest interface for applications needing only basic protection: sign only, encrypt only, sign-and-encrypt, or clear signing (where data is not modified and signature is returned separately).

The EV calls handle non-repudiation evidence, supporting proof of origin, proof of creation, proof of sender, proof of delivery, proof of receipt, and proof of approval. Evidence can be generated with or without the associated data included in the token. The GP calls are the most powerful, allowing fine-grained control over protection parameters and supporting simultaneous combinations of services. All three groups support both single-buffer and multi-buffer processing, allowing applications to process data streaming in from a network or reading from a file.
sections.eli5: You can just sign and encrypt (SE), or you can generate evidence that you sent something and when (EV), or you can do complex security combinations (GP). Pick what you need.

sections.title: Mechanism Independence and Algorithms
sections.content:
Like GSS-API, IDUP is mechanism-independent, supporting implementation with both secret-key and public-key cryptographic technologies. Applications are not tied to a specific underlying security mechanism. The RFC defines a Quality of Protection (QOP) parameter as a 32-bit field specifying which algorithms to use: the top 19 bits are reserved, followed by a 5-bit Type Specifier (strength qualifier), 4 bits for implementation-specific algorithms, and 4 bits for mechanism-specific algorithms.

For confidentiality, strength qualifiers include "strong" (80 bits or more effective key length), "medium" (40 to 80 bits), and "weak" (40 bits or less). For integrity, qualifiers distinguish between digital signatures and non-signature integrity (like MACs). The TS (Type Specifier) values are portable across mechanisms, while MA and IA values are mechanism and implementation specific. A receiver of a protected IDU returns QOP information showing which algorithm was used, allowing an application to understand what protection was applied.
sections.eli5: You can say "use strong encryption" and let the system pick the algorithm, or you can specify exactly which encryption you want. Different systems can all understand "strong" even if they use different algorithms.

sections.title: Time and Evidence Verification
sections.content:
IDUP mechanisms are encouraged to carry time information from the protector to the receivers, so recipients know when protection occurred. This is particularly important for non-repudiation evidence, where the time the evidence was generated may be critical for verification. Depending on platform resources, an IDUP environment may have access to trusted (secure) time, untrusted (local) time, both, or neither.

When requesting evidence protection, an application may specify which time services it wishes applied. For unprotection, an application may specify which kind of time to consult when validating the P-IDU. A receiver must know when protection occurred (or between what time bounds) to verify evidence correctly, especially for cases where key revocation or policy changes might have occurred between protection and verification. The RFC defines time as seconds elapsed since midnight, January 1, 1970, coordinated universal time.
sections.eli5: When you sign something with evidence, a timestamp might be included. If you try to verify it years later, you need to know roughly when it was signed to check if the keys were valid then. Some systems have trustworthy clocks, some just have local clocks.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
IDUP follows the security model of GSS-API. Confidentiality of media streams is achieved through encryption, which can be applied after compression in layered systems. For some applications, encrypting only the authentication or evidence tokens while leaving data in the clear may be acceptable, allowing different protection levels for different parts of the message.

The RFC notes that the described techniques do not introduce significant non-uniformity in receiver-side computational complexity that could enable denial-of-service attacks. Because protection and unprotection are independent operations with no forced synchronization or state sharing, attackers cannot force excessive computation through specially crafted sequences of operations.
sections.eli5: Security is handled the same way as in regular GSS-API. You can encrypt just parts of the message if you want. The design doesn't let attackers trick the system into doing wasteful work.
